newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish peace talks suspended for UK election.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish peace talks suspended for UK election.

text.p: Deadlocked Northern Ireland peace talks were adjourned on Wednesday to allow parties to prepare for a British general election seen as crucial to peace prospects in the troubled province.

Former U.S. senator George Mitchell, who has chaired the multiparty discussions for 10 months, said they would reconvene on June 3 after an election that British Prime Minister John Major must call by May 22 at the latest.

Major welcomed plans to restart the talks soon after the election and urged the Irish Republican Army (IRA) once more to lay down its arms and "credibly and verifiably" renew a ceasefire it broke more than a year ago.

IRA guerrillas, who have killed two British soldiers in Northern Ireland since last October, have said they are unlikely to call off armed action against British rule in the province before Britain has a new government.

Mitchell told a news conference that the province yearned for peace. "The overwhelming majority of people in Northern Ireland want a peaceful resolution and do not want a return to the bitterness and violence of the past," he said.
He said the parties had failed to reach agreement on how IRA guerrillas should dispose of arms in the event of a fresh truce, an issue that has dogged the talks for many months.
Mitchell's co-chairmen, General John de Chastelain of Canada and former Finnish Prime Minister Harri Holkeri, were alongside him when he spoke to reporters.

"In the circumstances, bearing in mind that the Easter holiday period will be followed in quick succession by a general election in the United Kingdom and district council elections in Northern Ireland, the independent chairmen proposed that the next plenary session be held on Tuesday 3 June," Mitchell said.

Britain says a 17-month IRA truce that collapsed a year ago was never meant to last. It is adamant that Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, will not get a seat at the talks until the guerrillas definitively end violence.

The multiparty talks have been plagued with difficulties since Britain and the Republic of Ireland launched them last June in a bid to find a political solution to the long-running conflict between the province's majority Protestants and the pro-Irish Catholic minority.

Clouded by IRA violence, an unstable ceasefire by Protestants guerrillas and deepening sectarianism in the province, they have made no headway on discussing key issues such as economic and political co-operation between the province and Catholic Ireland.
